title: Andal's garland
hookLine: a girl tries on the garland meant for God, and a singer is carried into the temple on a priest's shoulders
carry: God wants the love, in any language
tomorrow: a hunter breaks every rule. why does Shiva stop him?

cards: Every December and January, in the Tamil month of Margazhi, girls and women in Tamil Nadu, and in Tamil homes far from India, wake before dawn and sing thirty short verses.
A young woman wrote them about twelve hundred years ago. They call her friends to get up, bathe in the cold river, and go wake Krishna. It's a sleepover and a pilgrimage at once.
Her name was Andal. She's one of twelve poet-saints called the Alvars, and the only woman among them.

teach.b: The Alvars were Tamil poet-saints devoted to Vishnu, living roughly between the sixth and ninth centuries in the south of India. The name is usually explained as the ones immersed, drowned in God.
They didn't sing in Sanskrit, the language of priests.
They sang in Tamil, the language of home, and they came from every kind of background: a king, a chieftain turned highway robber turned devotee, a bard from a community kept outside the temple walls.
Their songs were later gathered into the Four Thousand Divine Hymns, still sung in Vishnu temples today. Two stories.
Andal, tradition says, was found as a baby under a tulsi plant by a temple priest, who raised her.
Every day he wove a garland for the god, and every day she secretly put it on first and looked at herself in the well, to see if she was beautiful enough for her beloved.
When the priest found out, he was horrified and made a fresh garland. That night, the story goes, the god told him in a dream: I want the one she wore.

Then Tiruppan Alvar, a singer from a community not allowed into the temple at Srirangam. He'd stand by the river, lost in song. One day a priest, needing to pass, threw a stone to move him and hit him.

teach.h: CARRIED IN ON A PRIEST'S SHOULDERS.
teach.b: That night, tradition says, the priest was told to carry the singer into the temple on his own shoulders. He did.

teach.h: GOD WANTS THE LOVE, IN ANY LANGUAGE.
teach.b: That's the Alvars' gift to bhakti: God, these stories teach, wants the love first, in the language of home, from anyone.

how: In Tamil Vishnu temples and Sri Vaishnava homes, the Alvars' hymns (the Nalayira Divya Prabandham) are sung daily, and Andal's thirty verses, the Tiruppavai, are sung before dawn through the month of Margazhi.

o: temple duties kept for trained Sanskrit-speaking priests
a secret teaching passed only from father to son
devotion to God, sung in your own language by anyone

p: wore the garland meant for God
carried in on a priest's shoulders

s: they sang in Tamil, the language of home, which was part of their power.
Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars
her thirty verses, the Tiruppavai, are still sung before dawn in Margazhi.
the Alvars all came from priestly families
tradition remembers a king, a reformed robber and a bard kept outside the temple.

games.q: you're the priest. you discover your daughter has been wearing God's garland before you offer it. you make a fresh one. that night, what does the story say you're told?
o: God wants the one she wore.
games.why: tradition says the god asked for the garland she'd worn. Andal is still called the one who gave the garland she had worn.

practice: Picture the edge of a room or a table where you weren't sure you belonged, and remember the singer by the river, singing anyway.
If you pray, say a few words to God now in the language you think in, the way the Alvars sang in Tamil: not perfect, just yours. If not, simply rest, and let the song matter more than the wall.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti yoga, through the Alvars: twelve Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu, immersed in God, singing in the language of home. Andal is the one woman among them.

orig.note: Tamil: alvar, usually explained as 'one immersed' (in God); the 'zh' is a Tamil sound between r and l.

carryVoice: Your line: God wants the love, in any language. Even a garland already worn can be the right gift. Day two sixty-nine, done.

sources.ref: hagiographies of Andal and Tiruppan Alvar (Sri Vaishnava tradition, e.g. the Guruparampara accounts)
